moves.pick: strayed loose on the moor
moves.why: A horse that vanished on the night of a struggle may simply have got loose and run off.
Holmes himself calls this belief a blunder: the horse has stayed hidden.

moves.pick: simpson
moves.why: The police have arrested Fitzroy Simpson, so he is the obvious suspect for taking the horse.

moves.pick: simpson
moves.why: Simpson is the man arrested; the natural guess is that he is the murderer.

moves.pick: one person took the horse and killed the trainer who got in the way
moves.why: Holmes expected the abductor to be the murderer; one thief who killed the trainer in his way fits both events.

moves.pick: he came to the stables on purpose
moves.why: A man who says he is lost knows that a stable-boy sleeps there alone every night.
He knows the stable routine, so his being lost is a pretext.

moves.pick: a drug for the boy's supper
moves.why: He wants the boy to have the paper tonight while the maid carries the boy's supper.

moves.pick: the dog made no noise
moves.why: A dog is kept in the stable, yet the lads in the loft heard nothing all night.
The trainer is found dead in a hollow and the horse is gone; this was no early exercise.
The trainer is found dead in a hollow and the horse is gone; this was no early exercise.

moves.pick: the_stranger
moves.why: Hunter is sure the stranger drugged his curry at the window, and the stranger had the chance.

moves.pick: simpson
moves.why: Simpson is a gentleman bookmaker lodging half a mile off with bets against the favourite; he fits the gentlemanly stranger after a tip.

moves.pick: Straker's own
moves.why: Simpson has no wound, and Holmes thinks it probable that Straker cut himself with his own knife.
If the cut came from Straker's own knife, no assailant need bear its mark.

moves.pick: simpson
moves.why: The police say Simpson got a duplicate key and opened the stable door.

moves.pick: to drug the lad and take the horse
moves.why: The police theory is that Simpson drugged the lad and led the horse away.

moves.pick: his own knife, as he fell
moves.why: Kicked on the forehead with the knife in his hand, Straker gashed his own thigh as he fell.

moves.pick: a drug for the boy's supper
moves.why: Simpson says it was a ten-pound note, and one was found in his purse: just what a tout offers a lad.

moves.pick: a ten-pound note
moves.why: A tout's bribe for a tip, and the note was still in his purse.

moves.pick: to drug the lad and take the horse
moves.why: If the paper was only a bribe, the one sign that he meant to drug the lad falls away.

moves.pick: only to get first-hand information
moves.why: He offered money for a tip, as a tout does, and kept the note.
Hunter never saw any drugging, and the paper was a banknote, not a drug.

moves.pick: strayed loose on the moor
moves.why: Still out: a loose horse would have been seen by now.

moves.pick: with the gypsies
moves.why: Gypsies camped within a mile on the night and were gone by Tuesday; Gregory thinks they may have the horse.

moves.pick: to hand him over to the gypsies
moves.why: Gregory's new element: Simpson was leading the horse to the gypsies when overtaken.

moves.pick: no part; they simply moved on
moves.why: Nothing links them to Simpson or the horse; a camp near a murder moves off, and the reward has them searching for the horse.

moves.pick: by habit, or to light his pipe
moves.why: He carried a pipe and tobacco; matches and a candle stub may just be what a smoker has in his pockets.
The knife's cork guard lay beside him: he had uncovered the blade at leisure, not in a sudden fight.
A delicate cataract knife, capped with cork, is not a weapon snatched up in haste.

moves.pick: straker
moves.why: Derbyshire's letters come to Straker's house, his bill was in Straker's pocket, and Mrs. Straker never had such a dress.

moves.pick: a woman Straker kept without his wife's knowledge
moves.why: The bill was in Straker's pocket, yet his wife never had such a costly dress.
Men do not carry a friend's bills; the 'friend' looks like Straker under another name.
A merely comfortable trainer secretly paying twenty-two guineas for a dress for another woman is living beyond his means.
Holmes has just come from London; 'that quite settles it' shows the garden-party was a test about the dress.
The costume was bait to see whether she owned dresses like those on the bill; she never had one.

moves.pick: he took it off for some task
moves.why: No wind, and the coat was laid across the bush; with the knife uncorked at leisure, he took it off himself to have his arms free.

moves.pick: straker
moves.why: Straker's pockets held a box of vestas and a candle; the match in the hollow is most likely his.

moves.pick: by habit, or to light his pipe
moves.why: Holmes went looking for a burnt match in the hollow and found it: a light was used down there.

moves.pick: to have a small light somewhere out on the moor
moves.why: A match was struck in the hollow, out of sight of the stable; the candle was for a light there.
Holmes firmly says to let the horse's name stand: he expects it alive and fit to run.

moves.pick: with the gypsies
moves.why: Gypsies clear out at trouble, could not sell such a horse, and would risk much for nothing.

moves.pick: to hand him over to the gypsies
moves.why: The gypsies could gain nothing from the horse, so Simpson had no reason to lead it to them.
Holmes shows the gypsies had no motive and every reason to keep clear.
The ground near the hollow is hard, but the horse's prints show plainly in the wet hollow towards Mapleton.

moves.pick: towards Mapleton
moves.why: Silver Blaze's own shoe fits a fresh print in the wet hollow on the line towards Mapleton, so the horse left the scene going that way.

moves.pick: one person took the horse and killed the trainer who got in the way
moves.why: The horse crossed the moor alone; nobody led it away from the killing.
Nobody led the horse from the hollow, so no abductor-murderer took it.

moves.pick: at Mapleton
moves.why: The horse and the man's tracks end at the gates of the Mapleton stables.

moves.pick: he meant to return the horse, then decided to keep it
moves.why: He set off towards King's Pyland, then came back and took the horse in at Mapleton's gates.
The horse's track goes straight in at Brown's own gates.

moves.pick: silas_brown
moves.why: Brown is always the first stirring at Mapleton, so he is the likeliest to have met the loose horse at dawn.

moves.pick: he found the horse loose and took it in
moves.why: The horse came alone near Mapleton, and Brown, first up, led it in at his gates.
After twenty minutes with Holmes, Brown comes out broken and obedient: the charge was true.

moves.pick: yes: he will be found fit and run on Tuesday
moves.why: Brown, broken, promises 'it shall be there', and Holmes insisted the name stay in the entries.

moves.pick: silver_blaze
moves.why: The tracks led in at Mapleton's gates and Brown is now taking Holmes's orders; 'it' is the horse.

moves.pick: at the race for the Wessex Cup on Tuesday
moves.why: Holmes told Ross to keep the horse entered; 'there' is the race.
Holmes read Brown's morning from the tracks and the square-toed boots, not by watching him.

moves.pick: put its appearance back as it was, after it had been altered
moves.why: Brown is an old horse-faker and the police search missed the horse: it has been altered, and 'change it' means undo that.

moves.pick: to do something to the horse himself
moves.why: He took an uncorked cataract knife and a candle, laid his coat aside, struck a light in the hollow, and the sheep by his villa are lame.

moves.pick: to make some fine cut on the horse
moves.why: A cataract knife for fine cuts, uncorked by Straker, with the horse beside him and the sheep lamed as if by practice.

moves.pick: to do something to him that could not be done in the stall
moves.why: A fine cut by match-light needed privacy, away from the lads in the loft.

moves.pick: someone cut their legs on purpose, practising for the horse
moves.why: Holmes expected lame sheep and calls it a singular epidemic; a fine knife on a horse is best practised first.
A man checking on his horses does not take a surgeon's blade and a candle and lead the horse out to a hollow.
Holmes treats the lameness as exceedingly important, a rehearsal for laming the horse.

moves.pick: nobody meant to carry him off: he was led out to be harmed and got loose
moves.why: Straker led the horse out to harm it, the horse struck him and ran off alone.

moves.pick: simpson
moves.why: The dog did nothing: the man who took the horse was one it knew, not the stranger it was set on that evening.

moves.pick: straker
moves.why: A familiar visitor with a key, door locked at nine and open at seven: Straker went out at one and died beside the horse.

moves.pick: simpson
moves.why: The silent dog rules out a stranger in the stable.

moves.pick: straker
moves.why: The dog knew the visitor, no duplicate key was found, and Straker had his own key.

moves.pick: the_stranger
moves.why: A stranger met by chance could not count on a curry to hide the opium; the man who took the horse came from the house.

moves.pick: straker
moves.why: Straker needed the lad asleep, and only Hunter's portion of the curry from his own house held opium.

moves.pick: simpson
moves.why: Simpson was never in the stable, the horse left the hollow alone, and Brown found it later.

moves.pick: silver_blaze
moves.why: Straker was cutting at the horse by match-light; the horse itself most likely lashed out and struck his head.

moves.pick: Simpson lost it and someone else had it
moves.why: Simpson was never in the hollow; Straker must have picked up the cravat Simpson says he lost.

moves.pick: the man who came in the night was someone the dog knew
moves.why: A guard dog set on the stranger that evening gave no alarm when the horse was taken.
The silent dog and the lone hoof-track leave no room for Simpson in the stable or leading the horse.
The dog knew the night visitor, and the horse left the hollow alone.
Simpson was a tout in the wrong place; the dog knew the man who came in the night.
The poisoning points to the house, not to Simpson, and the case against him falls apart.
No duplicate key was needed: Straker had his own.

moves.pick: the trainer was himself mixed up in what happened to the horse
moves.why: The silent dog points to Straker as the man who took the horse out, with a surgeon's knife and a light; the trainer was himself behind what happened to the horse.

moves.pick: silver_blaze
moves.why: Brown, a horse-faker, asked whether to 'change it' and Holmes said no; the plain bay in Ross's colours is Silver Blaze with his marks dyed.
Wash its face and leg in spirits of wine and it is Silver Blaze.
Holmes had found the horse before Ross spoke.
Holmes says he has laid hands on the murderer.

moves.pick: he meant to lame the favourite himself
moves.why: The horse acted in self-defence: Straker was attacking it with the cataract knife by match-light.
The horse killed him in self-defence; it was no murder.
Holmes admits he went down convinced of Simpson's guilt, and was wrong.
The horse broke away, but only after Straker himself took it out; someone did take it.

moves.pick: straker
moves.why: Straker's knife was meant for a tendon nick on the horse, and the lamed sheep are in his own paddock.
The cut came as he fell, not in convulsions after the blow.
The convulsion idea gives way to the knife gashing him as he fell.
Its convulsion version gives way: the knife cut him as he fell from the kick.
